title: Vomiting student
presenting_complaint: Two days of vomiting and abdominal pain, with increasing thirst and polyuria.
history: 19-year-old male university student with type 1 diabetes mellitus since age 11, on a basal-bolus insulin regimen. Two days of vomiting and abdominal pain; he stopped his insulin because he "wasn't eating". Increasing thirst and polyuria. No diarrhoea. Denies alcohol or drug use. No known drug allergies.

findings.name: Volume status / peripheral perfusion
findings.value: dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 4 s

findings.name: Venous blood gas
findings.value: pH 7.08, bicarbonate 7 mmol/L, glucose 28.4 mmol/L, potassium 5.6 mmol/L, lactate 2.1 mmol/L

diagnosis_options.label: Diabetic ketoacidosis
diagnosis_options.explanation: Type 1 diabetes with insulin omission, hyperglycaemia, ketonaemia and a severe metabolic acidosis (pH 7.08, bicarbonate 7 mmol/L) with ketonuria — the classic picture of diabetic ketoacidosis.

diagnosis_options.label: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state
diagnosis_options.explanation: Hyperglycaemia is right, but this is ketoacidosis: significant ketonaemia and a marked metabolic acidosis are present, which are not typical of HHS.

diagnosis_options.label: Acute pancreatitis
diagnosis_options.explanation: Abdominal pain and vomiting could suggest pancreatitis, but lipase is normal and the acidosis with ketones is explained by ketoacidosis.

diagnosis_options.label: Gastroenteritis
diagnosis_options.explanation: Vomiting and abdominal pain may mimic gastroenteritis, but there is no diarrhoea and the metabolic derangement indicates ketoacidosis.

diagnosis_options.label: Sepsis from urinary tract infection
diagnosis_options.explanation: Urinalysis shows no nitrites or leukocytes and there is no fever; the presentation is explained by ketoacidosis.

management_options.label: IV 0.9% saline resuscitation
management_options.explanation: Essential: this patient is markedly volume-depleted (dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 4 s, hypotension, tachycardia).

management_options.label: Fixed-rate IV insulin infusion 0.1 units/kg/h
management_options.explanation: Essential: a fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion is the standard treatment for diabetic ketoacidosis.

management_options.label: Continue long-acting basal insulin
management_options.explanation: Reasonable/indicated: continuing basal insulin helps avoid rebound ketosis when the infusion is stopped, but is not the primary intervention.

management_options.label: Potassium replacement guided by hourly levels once K+ falls below 5.5 mmol/L
management_options.explanation: Essential: total body potassium is depleted and levels will fall rapidly with insulin and fluids; replacement must be guided by hourly measurements.

management_options.label: IV sodium bicarbonate
management_options.explanation: Not recommended at this pH; bicarbonate therapy is potentially harmful in diabetic ketoacidosis.

management_options.label: Insulin bolus plus variable-rate sliding scale instead of a fixed-rate infusion
management_options.explanation: Harmful: a bolus with a variable-rate sliding scale is not the recommended approach; a fixed-rate infusion is required.
